original_question: In the semiregular hexagon with side lengths 2n-1, 2n, 2n-1, 2n, 2n-1, 2n, prove that the central location consisting of the two innermost triangles is covered by a lozenge in exactly one-third of all lozenge tilings. Equivalently, in the dual honeycomb graph, prove that a uniformly random perfect matching contains the central edge with probability exactly 1/3.
target_in_paper: Section 2 ("Lozenges"), Problem 1 of Propp's paper: show that in the 2n-1, 2n, 2n-1 semiregular hexagon, the central location consisting of the two innermost triangles is covered by a lozenge in exactly one-third of the tilings.
correct_elements: Your draft captures the main mathematical content of the target problem very well: it asks for the exact one-third proportion, it identifies the central location as the two innermost triangles, and it includes the paper's own equivalent perfect-matching reformulation in the dual honeycomb graph. It also stays narrowly focused on the original lozenge-tiling question rather than broadening to later generalizations.
missing_details: The cyclic side-length data are not paper-faithful as written. In Section 2, Propp defines an a,b,c semiregular hexagon to have side lengths a,b,c,a,b,c in cyclic order. Thus the paper's "2n-1, 2n, 2n-1 semiregular hexagon" means side lengths (2n-1, 2n, 2n-1, 2n-1, 2n, 2n-1), not the alternating six-term list in the draft.
The region is a semiregular hexagon with all interior angles equal to 120 degrees, drawn on the triangular lattice.
The quantifier should be explicit: the statement is for every positive integer n.
A lozenge should be defined as a unit rhombus formed by two adjacent unit equilateral triangles.
The graph-theoretic reformulation should specify that the dual graph is the finite honeycomb graph dual to the dissection of the hexagon into unit triangles.
The "central edge" should be identified as the edge of that dual graph joining the two vertices corresponding to the two innermost triangles.
The probability statement should explicitly be with respect to the uniform distribution on all lozenge tilings, equivalently on all perfect matchings.

No ambient ring/field, homogeneity condition, degree restriction, nilpotency assumption, operator definition, or asymptotic phrase such as "for all sufficiently large m" belongs to this problem; the only relevant global quantifier is over positive integers n.
refined_question: For each positive integer n, let H_n be the semiregular hexagon on the triangular lattice with side lengths 2n-1, 2n, 2n-1, 2n-1, 2n, 2n-1 in cyclic order (equivalently, the 2n-1, 2n, 2n-1 semiregular hexagon), and let C_n denote its central location, i.e. the pair of innermost unit triangles. Show that exactly one-third of the lozenge tilings of H_n contain the lozenge covering C_n.
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, if G_n is the finite honeycomb graph dual to the unit-triangle dissection of H_n, then a uniformly random perfect matching of G_n contains the edge joining the two vertices corresponding to the two innermost triangles with probability exactly 1/3.
justification: The draft is targeting Problem 1 almost verbatim: the one-third claim and the parenthetical perfect-matching reformulation both match Propp's official wording in Section 2. The main correction needed is geometric: Propp's notation for a semiregular hexagon is defined earlier in the same section as side lengths a,b,c,a,b,c, so the intended region is the 2n-1, 2n, 2n-1 semiregular hexagon in that sense, not the alternating six-side sequence written in the draft. I therefore kept the question at the exact scope of Problem 1 and did not broaden it to the later Ciucu-Krattenthaler generalization mentioned in the progress paragraph, except insofar as that paragraph confirms that the special case a=2n-1, b=2n solves this precise problem. Since the problem is purely combinatorial, algebraic items such as ambient field or degree conditions are inapplicable here.
